status: Four prepared source-based biological structure/force cases resolve this authoring duty through unchanged claims, not observed learner success or complete adaptation mastery.

swamp-roots.locator: 15 June 2026 main habitat and adaptation paragraphs
swamp-roots.readScope: Complete short main body read; photographs not visually assessed.
swamp-roots.facts: Waterlogged unstable soil is the context; buttresses and stilt roots provide support. Breathing roots have a distinct function.

mangrove-roots.locator: 1 July 2026, All about mangrove roots, buttress and stilt sections
mangrove-roots.readScope: Main habitat, four root-type and conservation sections read; no linked storymap or image inspection claim.
mangrove-roots.facts: Flared bases support tall trees; stilt roots stabilise plants in soft wet ground. Pencil/knee roots support gas exchange, not automatically the same mechanical role.

root-anchorage.locator: Introduction, Quick facts, windrock explanation and Aftercare
root-anchorage.readScope: Complete main advice text read, no image or linked article inspection.
root-anchorage.facts: Developing roots anchor a tree; wind movement can loosen/damage roots. Staking temporarily supplements support while the root system establishes. No pupil staking activity is proposed.

shell-mechanics.locator: Hu, Sielert and Gordon (2011), printed 1197–1204, especially section 4.1
shell-mechanics.readScope: Abstract/introduction/methods and turtle model/limits text read. No figure inspection or full-paper visual claim; numerical scaling is not taught.
shell-mechanics.facts: Museum shell geometry and a simplified model are consistent with resistance to predator bites; sufficiently strong predators can break shells. This is bounded model evidence, not a direct live bite test or universal protection.

porcupine.locator: ABOUT, rigid quills/defensive response/no shooting/unprotected underside paragraphs
porcupine.readScope: Complete main text read; no image/video inspected.
porcupine.facts: Rigid defensive quills can puncture a contacting threat, discouraging attack. Quills are not fired, and some predators can reach the unprotected underside.

buttress.given: A rainforest/swamp tree has broad plank-like buttresses at its base, in the unstable wet-soil setting described by NParks. A supplied original wind-load diagram shows an external sideways push; it is a model, not a measured storm outcome.
buttress.feature: The spreading basal extensions support and brace the tree.
buttress.harmfulForce: Sideways loading that can cause leaning or overturning.
buttress.mechanism: Support at the base helps keep the tall tree steady against this loading; connect the given force to support rather than only naming water/nutrient uptake.
buttress.limit: NParks supports the support function; this is not proof of a failure threshold or that every rainforest soil/root system has identical depth or conditions.

stilt-root.given: A mangrove grows with stilt-like roots spreading from above the ground into soft wet soil, as in the NParks account. Compare it with the separately described pencil roots.
stilt-root.feature: Stilt roots spread into the ground to stabilise the plant.
stilt-root.harmfulForce: Loads tending to tip or shift a tall plant in soft ground.
stilt-root.mechanism: The supporting root arrangement helps the plant remain stable. Distinguish this from an upright pencil root whose stated function is gas exchange, not assume every above-ground root protects mechanically.
stilt-root.limit: No storm speed, identical soil strength, force measurement or claim that any root shape prevents every storm loss is supplied.

turtle.given: A turtle has a rigid shell covering vulnerable body regions. The study reports measured shell geometry and a model relating shell strength to predator bites; its discussion also records that some strong predators break shells.
turtle.feature: A relatively rigid surrounding shell forms a physical barrier.
turtle.mechanism: The shell can resist biting loads and protect tissue when the load does not exceed its capacity; the bite force does not magically disappear.
turtle.limit: Do not infer that every shell is unbreakable, that every turtle retracts its head, or that the authors performed live predator tests. No quantitative shell equation is required.

porcupine.given: A porcupine has rigid quills on its back and rump. The zoo describes quills contacting potential threats and an underside that is not similarly covered.
porcupine.feature: Sharp rigid quills stand out towards a contacting predator.
porcupine.harmfulForce: An attacking predator’s bite or bodily contact that could injure the animal.
porcupine.mechanism: Contact with the sharp quills can hurt/deter the attacker, reducing its access to the protected body. This is a defensive-contact mechanism, not a claim that quills absorb all the bite force like a cushion.
porcupine.limit: Quills are not shot. The animal remains vulnerable, including at the underside; neither having quills nor having a shell guarantees survival.

actions: Actually use both plant cases and both animal cases. Identify the physical trait, the specified harmful loading/contact, how the trait reduces harm and one supported limit. Source cards remain available; no new species-fact recall inventory is imposed.

Construct and defend a structure→mechanism→protection argument for each kind of organism. Contrast a supporting root with a breathing root and shell resistance with quill deterrence, rather than merely labelling all traits adaptations.

Changed case: an original unfamiliar-organism brief supplies a broad stabilising base, a thin gas-exchange tube and no loading/strength data. Explain which feature could address tipping, which does a different job, and what cannot be concluded. Do not infer a guaranteed wind threshold.
Reject a tempting explanation that a turtle’s shell removes the bite force or a porcupine shoots quills. Repair it using the actual source evidence and keep the limits.
protocol.positive: Both plant/animal plurality and named-force→feature→mechanism reasoning, with source-grounded uncertainty.
protocol.nearMiss: Only explains water loss/light access, calls every root support, names a shell without the bite relation, or assumes a trait guarantees survival.
protocol.transfer: A changed supplied feature/load account is interpreted by function and evidence, with insufficient facts identified.

wholeClaimBoundary: Rainforest Plant Adaptations retains its whole existing drip-tip, buttress, epiphyte, liana and adaptation requirements. Only its support/anchorage component contributes here; neither stilt roots nor this task silently widens that card.

Structures for Survival retains actual argument construction, internal/external structures and non-defence functions. These protection cases contribute a selected component; they do not certify its entire internal/reproduction/growth inventory. Its full existing plant-parts and skeleton/muscle readiness is retained.

No organism handling, harmful live loading or deliberate damage is required. Verbal source evidence and original safe representations account for this descriptive source duty; any complete-topic observation tasks remain separate.
consumerBoundary: All current IDs, claims, guides, contexts, ages and dependencies unchanged; no learner/mastery transfer. Historical confidence flags are not freshly certified.
